part_title: Translation, Speech Transcription and Polly Voices
review_basis: Original AIF Module 08 numbered WebPs visually inspected one by one on 2026-11-14; rewritten concise visual-first narration based on actual diagram order, figures, examples and visible caveats; fresh audio required.

scenes.title: Amazon Translate
scenes.narration: Follow the top row from left to right. An English product message, 'Your order is ready,' enters Amazon Translate. The service converts the text to Spanish, illustrated as 'Tu pedido está listo,' for a localized website. The final green panel reminds us that important customer-facing wording should be checked by a person for meaning and tone. The lower-left example is the same English-to-Spanish API request and response. In the center, compare three language services by the direction of conversion. Translate changes written text into another written language. Transcribe changes speech audio into written text. Polly changes written text into speech audio. These are not interchangeable just because they work with language. The lower-right knowledge-base example shows that translated articles can help international customers find information in their own language. Ask which format you already have and which format you need. Translation does not automatically guarantee correct legal, technical or culturally sensitive wording, so review those outputs.

scenes.title: Amazon Transcribe
scenes.narration: The top-left box is a recorded customer call, not text. Amazon Transcribe applies automatic speech recognition, or ASR, to convert the spoken words into a transcript. Optional language identification can select a supported language, and supported PII redaction can obscure personal information such as phone numbers. The right side shows a timestamped transcript that can feed a searchable call archive or captions. Look at the worked example below: the customer says, 'My order is delayed.' The output associates 'My order' with 00:00:00.000 and 'is delayed' with 00:00:01.250. Those timestamps help locate speech in the recording. Finally compare the exam cards. Transcribe starts with audio and returns text; Polly starts with text and returns spoken audio. Redaction is a configured capability, not a guarantee that every sensitive detail was found, so privacy-sensitive workflows still need checks. For searching thousands of recorded support calls, first transcribe them.

scenes.title: Transcribe – Toxicity Detection
scenes.narration: This five-stage diagram is a human moderation workflow for prerecorded US English audio. First comes a recorded support call. Second, Amazon Transcribe runs a batch job with toxicity detection enabled, not a live real-time call decision. Third, the sample transcript shows segments from zero to eight seconds with no detected toxicity, eight to fifteen seconds with a possible insult marked high confidence, and fifteen to twenty-seven seconds with none. Fourth, a person reviews the highlighted segment, its context and company policy. Fifth, that person decides appropriate next steps; the service does not automatically punish anyone. In the lower example the possible insult is a detection result, not a final judgment about intent. The right-hand table emphasizes segment timestamps, categories and confidence. High confidence means the detector is more confident in its classification, not that the context has been understood perfectly. This distinction matters for safe moderation: use the output to prioritize review rather than treating it as proof.

scenes.title: Amazon Transcribe – Improving Accuracy
scenes.narration: Begin with the audio phrase 'AsterValve inspection.' A normal speech recognizer may mistakenly transcribe the unfamiliar product name as 'a star valve inspection,' as the lower example illustrates. The upper diagram shows two ways to improve domain accuracy. A custom vocabulary supplies particular phrases, such as AsterValve, and optional display formatting. A custom language model uses a larger collection of domain-specific text to learn typical terminology and wording in context. The lower-left comparison shows the same phrase with each approach and a combined example. These are illustrative results: you must actually measure error rates on representative audio instead of assuming that every customization works. On the right, use custom vocabulary when there is a manageable list of brand names, acronyms or special terms. Use a custom language model when the vocabulary and phrasing of a whole domain differ from general speech. The goal is accurate transcripts for search, call analytics and service workflows, not just a better-looking word on one demonstration.

scenes.title: Amazon Polly
scenes.narration: Read the four boxes along the top. A mobile application supplies the text 'Your package is ready.' Amazon Polly synthesizes it into spoken audio, shown as an MP3-style audio output. The app plays the sound to its user. This is text-to-speech, useful when someone needs a voice notification or an accessibility feature. The lower-left worked example repeats those three stages with the same message. The center panel adds the application choices: provide text, select a supported language and voice, request speech generation and play the returned audio. Polly does not recognize what a caller has spoken; that is Amazon Transcribe. Polly also does not automatically translate a sentence into another language; Amazon Translate handles text translation. Keep the formats straight: the request is readable text and the result is sound. A simple decision check: if an app must read order-status messages aloud, the required managed AWS service is Polly.

scenes.title: Polly – Advanced Features
scenes.narration: This slide builds on basic Polly speech generation. On the left, the input text is 'Welcome to AWS.' A pronunciation lexicon can instruct Polly to pronounce AWS as 'Amazon Web Services' instead of reading the letters differently. SSML, a speech markup language, can add delivery instructions such as a pause. Select a compatible voice for the requested features. The top-right boxes show two different outputs obtained through separate synthesis requests: spoken audio and speech marks containing timing information, where supported. Now follow the reading-application example along the bottom. First request the spoken file, then request speech marks, then use word timing to highlight the matching word while the audio plays. The right-hand summary separates the concepts: lexicon controls pronunciation, SSML controls speech delivery and speech marks provide timing for synchronization. Do not assume every voice supports every feature; check compatibility before designing a reading assistant.
